title: The Production Environment at Google, from the Viewpoint of an SRE
subtitle: Follow a request through scheduling, discovery, storage, and capacity
summary: Pip’s booking process restarts on another machine. The crew separates resource identity, running tasks, stable names, and durable storage. Scheduling and capacity must account for correlated failures and the traffic that survives while replacements start.

concepts.title: Machines, servers, jobs, and tasks
concepts.body: Pip mistakes a machine for the booking server running on it. In the chapter, a machine is physical or virtual capacity; a server is a service-providing program. Borg jobs describe work, and tasks are individual running copies. Pip can move a failed task without permanently tying the service to one host.

concepts.title: Scheduling and failure domains
concepts.body: Pip puts four booking replicas on one rack and loses them with its switch. Borg schedules resource requests and supervises execution, but placement must consider correlated failure. Pip spreads replicas across failure domains. Enough surviving capacity must serve requests while crashed tasks are replaced.

concepts.title: Discovery, storage, and coordination
concepts.body: Pip’s rescheduled task still calls an obsolete address. BNS provides stable-name indirection; Chubby supports consistent coordination and naming information. Durable data belongs in shared storage rather than task-local scratch space. Pip distinguishes Colossus, Bigtable, and Spanner as different storage layers and consistency choices, not interchangeable tools.

concepts.title: A request consumes regional capacity
concepts.body: Pip estimates capacity for 750 booking requests per second. At 80 requests per task, ten tasks cover demand before spares. The chapter’s search example combines offline indexing, online serving, load balancing, and regional replicas. Pip adds maintenance and failure headroom, checking destination capacity and latency before shifting regions.

misconceptions.claim: A server name identifies a permanent physical machine.
misconceptions.correction: Here a server is software; task discovery follows it when the scheduler changes its placement.

misconceptions.claim: Enough total replicas guarantee failure tolerance.
misconceptions.correction: Replicas must also span relevant failure domains and leave enough usable capacity after a failure.

scenario.title: Place work on shared machines
scenario.context: A cluster has homogeneous machines but a memory-heavy indexing job competes with latency-sensitive search servers. The scheduler can place both through a shared resource allocator or reserve machines by service.

options.label: Use shared allocation with explicit requests
options.benefit: Unused capacity can serve either workload and placement stays adaptable.
options.cost: Bad requests can cause noisy-neighbor pressure unless monitored.
options.consequence: The team measures saturation and adjusts requests as demand changes.

options.label: Reserve dedicated machines
options.benefit: Latency-sensitive work gets predictable headroom and simpler local diagnosis.
options.cost: Reservation strands capacity and makes hardware growth expensive.
options.consequence: Search remains stable, but idle reserved machines lower overall utilization.

scenario.debrief: Shared allocation trades local predictability for adaptable capacity; resource requests and health evidence decide whether the trade remains safe.

quiz.question: A Borg task moves to another host. What lets clients keep finding it?
options: Its stable task name resolved through BNS
A promise never to restart it
quiz.explanation: Naming indirection separates logical task identity from its current host and port.

quiz.question: A task serves 100 QPS and peak demand is 950 QPS. How many tasks cover one update plus one simultaneous task failure?
quiz.explanation: Ten tasks serve the peak; two additional tasks cover the two unavailable copies.

quiz.question: Why put a copy of a read-heavy search index near each serving region?
options: To reduce remote-read latency and provide regional resilience
To eliminate the need for frontend load balancing
To make local scratch disks durable
quiz.explanation: Regional storage avoids cross-region reads and provides additional copies of the dataset.
